lessons.title: The Grand Alliance & the Origins of the Cold War
lessons.description: How wartime allies became Cold War enemies through conferences, ideology and the atomic bomb.
lessons.content_html:
The Grand Alliance

During the Second World War, the USA, Britain and the Soviet Union formed the Grand Alliance to defeat Nazi Germany. Despite their shared enemy, the three powers had very different political systems and deep suspicions of each other. Understanding these tensions is essential for explaining why the Cold War began almost as soon as the fighting stopped.

Key Fact

The Grand Alliance was held together by a common enemy — Nazi Germany. Once that enemy was defeated, the ideological differences between capitalism and communism resurfaced and drove the superpowers apart.

Ideological Differences

The USA was a capitalist democracy. It believed in free elections, freedom of speech, and private enterprise. The Soviet Union was a communist state. It believed the state should own all industry and land, and a single party — the Communist Party — should rule. These ideologies were fundamentally opposed: each side saw the other as a threat to its way of life.

Stalin believed capitalist countries would eventually try to destroy communism. Truman believed communism destroyed individual freedom and had to be contained. Churchill, though initially allied with Stalin, warned in his 1946 “Iron Curtain” speech that Soviet expansion threatened European liberty.

Stalin was deeply suspicious of the West. The USSR had suffered around 27 million deaths in the war, and Stalin wanted a buffer zone of friendly states in Eastern Europe to prevent future invasion. Roosevelt (and later Truman) wanted to spread democracy and free trade globally; Truman was far more hostile to communism than Roosevelt had been. Churchill feared Soviet expansion but needed American support to rebuild Britain’s war-shattered economy.

The Wartime Conferences

The Grand Alliance met at three major conferences to plan the post-war world. Each conference revealed growing tensions between the allies.

November 1943

Tehran Conference

The first meeting of Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill. They agreed to open a second front in France (D-Day, June 1944) and that the USSR would declare war on Japan after Germany’s defeat. The atmosphere was broadly cooperative, though Stalin resented the delayed second front.

February 1945

Yalta Conference

With Germany close to defeat, the “Big Three” agreed to divide Germany into four zones of occupation, hold free elections in liberated countries, set up the United Nations, and allow the USSR to enter the war against Japan. Stalin agreed to free elections in Poland, though the meaning of “free” would soon be disputed.

July–August 1945

Potsdam Conference

Roosevelt had died and was replaced by Truman, who was far more suspicious of Soviet intentions. Churchill lost the 1945 election halfway through and was replaced by Attlee. Disagreements emerged over Poland’s western border, German reparations, and the future of Eastern Europe. Truman revealed the successful test of the atomic bomb during the conference, increasing Soviet suspicion.

Key Fact

The three conferences — Tehran (1943), Yalta (February 1945) and Potsdam (July 1945) — show a clear pattern: cooperation gave way to suspicion, then open disagreement as the common enemy disappeared.

The Impact of the Atomic Bomb

In August 1945, the USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, forcing Japan’s surrender. The bomb transformed superpower relations in several ways.

First, it gave the USA a monopoly on nuclear weapons, making it the most powerful country in the world. Second, Truman used the bomb partly to intimidate the Soviet Union — a tactic historians call “atomic diplomacy.” Third, Stalin felt threatened and accelerated the Soviet nuclear programme. The USSR tested its own atomic bomb in 1949, launching the arms race.

Truman told Stalin about the bomb at Potsdam but gave no details. Stalin already knew about it through Soviet spies. The bomb made Stalin feel the USA could bully the USSR, so he was determined to develop his own. This mutual suspicion fuelled the arms race and deepened the divide between East and West. Some historians argue the bomb was dropped on Japan partly to demonstrate American power to the Soviets, not just to end the Pacific War.

From Alliance to Rivalry

By late 1945, the Grand Alliance was effectively over. The wartime need for cooperation had gone, and the ideological gulf between capitalism and communism dominated. Truman saw Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe as aggression; Stalin saw it as self-defence. Neither side trusted the other, and both began preparing for a long struggle — the Cold War.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For “Explain One Consequence” questions (4 marks), identify a clear consequence, then develop it with specific detail. For example: “One consequence of the Potsdam Conference was increased distrust between the superpowers. This was because Truman revealed the atomic bomb to Stalin, making Stalin feel the USA could use its nuclear monopoly as a bargaining tool. As a result, Stalin accelerated the Soviet nuclear programme, which deepened tensions.” Always link cause to effect with connectives like “this meant that” or “as a result.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Grand Alliance was a temporary partnership held together by the need to defeat Nazi Germany — once that enemy was gone, ideological differences resurfaced.
  • The three conferences (Tehran, Yalta, Potsdam) show a clear shift from cooperation to suspicion and disagreement, especially after Roosevelt’s death and Truman’s harder line against the USSR.
  • The atomic bomb gave the USA a decisive advantage, but it also accelerated Soviet efforts to build their own bomb, launching the arms race that defined the Cold War.

lessons.title: The Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan & Berlin Blockade
lessons.description: How containment, economic aid and the Berlin Crisis divided Europe into two hostile blocs.
lessons.content_html:
The Long & Novikov Telegrams

In 1946, two influential documents hardened attitudes on both sides. George Kennan’s Long Telegram from Moscow warned that the Soviet Union was determined to expand and could not be trusted. He recommended a policy of firm “containment” — stopping communism from spreading any further. Shortly after, the Soviet ambassador Nikolai Novikov sent his own telegram to Moscow, arguing that the USA was building up its military power to dominate the world and destroy communism. Both telegrams reinforced the growing distrust between the superpowers.

Soviet Satellite States

Between 1945 and 1948, Stalin established communist governments across Eastern Europe. Countries like Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Romania and Bulgaria became satellite states — officially independent but in reality controlled by Moscow. Stalin used rigged elections, intimidation and the presence of the Red Army to install loyal communist leaders. He saw this buffer zone as essential protection against future invasion from the West.

Key Fact

By 1948, almost every country in Eastern Europe had a Soviet-controlled communist government. The USA saw this as aggressive expansion; Stalin saw it as defensive — creating a buffer zone to protect the USSR from future attack.

The Truman Doctrine (1947)

In March 1947, President Truman announced the Truman Doctrine. He declared that the USA would support any country threatened by a communist takeover. This was triggered by the crisis in Greece, where communist rebels were fighting to overthrow the government and Britain could no longer afford to provide military support. Truman asked Congress for $400 million in aid for Greece and Turkey.

The Truman Doctrine was significant because it formally committed the USA to the policy of containment — stopping communism from spreading, even if it meant intervening in other countries. It marked the end of American isolationism and divided the world into two camps: capitalist West and communist East.

The Marshall Plan (1947)

In June 1947, Secretary of State George Marshall announced a massive programme of economic aid for Europe. The Marshall Plan provided $12.7 billion to help war-devastated European countries rebuild their economies. The USA believed that poverty and instability made countries vulnerable to communism — if people were hungry and desperate, communist ideas became attractive.

Stalin saw the Marshall Plan as “dollar imperialism” — an attempt to buy the loyalty of European countries and draw them into the American sphere of influence. He banned Eastern European satellite states from accepting Marshall Aid. Czechoslovakia initially wanted to accept the aid but was forced by Stalin to refuse. In response, Stalin set up Comecon (the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance) in 1949 to coordinate the economies of the communist bloc.

Cominform & Comecon

Stalin responded to Western containment with two organisations. Cominform (1947) coordinated communist parties across Europe and ensured they followed Moscow’s line. It tightened Soviet control over the satellite states. Comecon (1949) was the economic equivalent — it coordinated trade and industry across the communist bloc. Together, these organisations deepened the division of Europe into two hostile camps.

The Berlin Blockade & Airlift (1948–49)

Germany and its capital Berlin were divided into four zones of occupation after the war. Berlin lay deep inside the Soviet zone, but the western sectors of the city were controlled by the USA, Britain and France. In June 1948, the Western allies introduced a new currency (the Deutschmark) into their zones to help economic recovery. Stalin saw this as a threat and responded by blocking all road, rail and canal links into West Berlin — the Berlin Blockade.

Key Fact

The Berlin Airlift lasted 318 days (June 1948 – May 1949). The Western allies flew over 275,000 flights, delivering 2.3 million tonnes of supplies to the 2 million people of West Berlin. At its peak, a plane landed every 90 seconds.

Stalin lifted the blockade in May 1949, having failed to force the Western allies out. The crisis had three major consequences: Germany was formally divided into the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG / West Germany) and the German Democratic Republic (GDR / East Germany); NATO (the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation) was formed in April 1949 as a Western military alliance; and the Cold War division of Europe became permanent.

NATO was a military alliance of Western nations formed in 1949. Its key principle was collective security — an attack on one member was an attack on all. Original members included the USA, Britain, France, Canada and eight other nations. The Soviet response came in 1955 with the formation of the Warsaw Pact. The FRG (West Germany) was established in May 1949 as a capitalist, democratic state aligned with the West. The GDR (East Germany) was established in October 1949 as a communist state controlled by the Soviet Union.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For “Write a Narrative Account” questions (8 marks), structure your answer chronologically and show how one event led to the next. For example, link the Long Telegram → Truman Doctrine → Marshall Plan → Soviet response (Cominform/Comecon) → Berlin Blockade. Use connectives like “this led to,” “as a consequence,” and “this was significant because” to show analytical links, not just description.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Truman Doctrine (1947) committed the USA to containing communism, ending isolationism and dividing the world into two camps.
  • The Marshall Plan provided $12.7 billion to rebuild Western Europe — Stalin saw it as dollar imperialism and banned satellite states from accepting aid, deepening the East-West divide.
  • The Berlin Blockade and Airlift (1948–49) was the first major crisis of the Cold War, leading to the permanent division of Germany and the formation of NATO.

lessons.title: The Arms Race & the Hungarian Uprising 1956
lessons.description: How nuclear weapons, the Warsaw Pact and Hungary's failed revolt intensified the Cold War.
lessons.content_html:
The Arms Race

The arms race was one of the most dangerous features of the Cold War. After the USA dropped atomic bombs on Japan in 1945, it held a nuclear monopoly. However, in 1949 the Soviet Union tested its own atomic bomb — far earlier than the Americans expected. This shocked the USA and triggered a cycle of escalation that lasted decades.

Key Fact

The USA tested the first hydrogen bomb in 1952 — a weapon 1,000 times more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb. The USSR tested its own hydrogen bomb just a year later in 1953. By the late 1950s, both sides had developed intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), meaning each superpower could destroy the other in minutes.

The arms race created a balance of terror known as Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD). Neither side could attack without being destroyed in return, so nuclear war became too dangerous to risk. While MAD prevented direct conflict, it also meant the world lived under the constant threat of annihilation.

The Formation of the Warsaw Pact (1955)

In 1955, the Soviet Union formed the Warsaw Pact — a military alliance of communist countries in Eastern Europe. This was a direct response to West Germany joining NATO in the same year. The Warsaw Pact bound the satellite states to the USSR militarily, giving the Soviet Union the right to station troops across Eastern Europe.

NATO (1949) was a voluntary alliance of Western nations committed to collective security. Members included the USA, Britain, France, Canada and others. The Warsaw Pact (1955) was the communist equivalent, but membership was not voluntary — it was imposed by Moscow. Together, these two alliances divided Europe into armed camps. If war broke out, every member of each alliance was bound to fight, turning any local conflict into a potential world war.

Events Leading to the Hungarian Uprising (1956)

Hungary had been a Soviet satellite state since 1948, governed by the brutal Stalinist leader Mátyás Rákosi. Hungarians resented Soviet control: the secret police terrorised the population, living standards were poor, and Hungarian resources were exported to the USSR. When Stalin died in 1953, his successor Khrushchev gave a “Secret Speech” in February 1956 denouncing Stalin’s crimes. This encouraged hopes of reform across Eastern Europe.

In Poland, workers’ protests in June 1956 led to the appointment of the reformer Gomulka, who was accepted by Khrushchev. Inspired by Poland’s example, Hungarian students and workers began demanding change: they wanted free elections, the withdrawal of Soviet troops, and the return of the reformist leader Imre Nagy.

The Hungarian Uprising

23 October 1956

The Uprising Begins

Students and workers took to the streets of Budapest. They tore down a giant statue of Stalin and attacked the secret police headquarters. Soviet troops initially withdrew from the city.

24 October – 1 November 1956

Nagy Takes Power

Imre Nagy became Prime Minister. He announced reforms: free elections, the end of one-party rule, and — crucially — Hungary’s withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact. This was a step too far for Khrushchev.

4 November 1956

Soviet Invasion

Khrushchev sent 1,000 tanks and 200,000 troops into Budapest. Fierce street fighting lasted two weeks. Around 2,500 Hungarians were killed, 200,000 fled as refugees, and Nagy was arrested. He was later executed in 1958.

Key Fact

The USSR crushed the Hungarian Uprising because Nagy announced Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact. Khrushchev could accept limited reform, but losing a satellite state from the military alliance would weaken Soviet control of Eastern Europe and encourage other countries to break away.

International Reaction

The Western response was limited. The USA condemned the Soviet invasion publicly and accepted Hungarian refugees, but did not intervene militarily. President Eisenhower was unwilling to risk nuclear war over Hungary. Britain and France were distracted by the Suez Crisis in Egypt. The United Nations debated the crisis but could take no action because the USSR used its veto in the Security Council.

The USA’s policy of containment meant preventing the spread of communism, not removing it where it already existed. Hungary was already inside the Soviet sphere of influence. Direct military intervention would have risked nuclear war. The Suez Crisis also diverted British and French attention. The lack of Western intervention sent a clear message to Eastern Europe: the West would not risk war to liberate Soviet satellite states.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For “Explain Importance” questions (8 marks), always explain importance in relation to the wider situation. For example, don’t just describe what happened in Hungary — explain what difference it made for the Cold War. Did it change how the superpowers behaved? Did it affect other countries? Did it change international relations? The best answers connect the event to broader developments.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The arms race escalated from atomic to hydrogen bombs and ICBMs, creating Mutually Assured Destruction — neither side could attack without being destroyed in return.
  • The Warsaw Pact (1955) formalised the military division of Europe and gave the USSR the right to station troops in Eastern European satellite states.
  • The Hungarian Uprising (1956) showed that the USSR would use force to maintain control of its satellite states, and that the West would not intervene to liberate them.

lessons.title: The Berlin Wall & the Cuban Missile Crisis
lessons.description: How the Berlin Wall and the Cuban Missile Crisis brought the world to the brink of nuclear war.
lessons.content_html:
The Berlin Refugee Problem

By the late 1950s, Berlin had become a flashpoint of Cold War tension. West Berlin was a thriving capitalist outpost deep inside communist East Germany, and it was a constant embarrassment to the Soviet Union. Between 1949 and 1961, around 3 million East Germans fled to the West through Berlin — many of them skilled workers, doctors and engineers whose departure weakened the East German economy. This refugee crisis was humiliating for Khrushchev because it showed that people preferred capitalism to communism.

Khrushchev’s Berlin Ultimatum (1958)

In November 1958, Khrushchev issued an ultimatum to the Western powers: they must leave West Berlin within six months, or he would hand control of all access routes to East Germany. The West refused. A series of summit meetings followed, but none resolved the crisis.

Camp David (1959): Khrushchev and Eisenhower met in a relatively friendly atmosphere. Khrushchev withdrew his ultimatum, but no agreement was reached on Berlin. Paris (1960): The summit collapsed when the USSR shot down an American U-2 spy plane over Soviet territory. Eisenhower refused to apologise, and Khrushchev walked out. Vienna (1961): The new US President Kennedy met Khrushchev. Kennedy was inexperienced and Khrushchev bullied him, reissuing his Berlin ultimatum. Kennedy left shaken, saying it was the “worst thing in my life.”

The Construction of the Berlin Wall (1961)

On 13 August 1961, East German soldiers began sealing the border between East and West Berlin with barbed wire, which was quickly replaced by a concrete wall. The Berlin Wall was heavily guarded with watchtowers, searchlights, minefields and a “death strip” where guards had orders to shoot anyone trying to cross.

Key Fact

The Berlin Wall stopped the flow of refugees almost overnight. It solved the USSR’s refugee problem, but it became the most powerful symbol of the Cold War division of Europe. At least 140 people were killed trying to cross the Wall between 1961 and 1989.

Kennedy protested but did not try to tear the Wall down. He recognised that a wall was preferable to a war. In June 1963, Kennedy visited West Berlin and delivered his famous “Ich bin ein Berliner” speech, declaring American solidarity with the people of West Berlin. The Wall remained in place for 28 years.

The Cuban Revolution & the Bay of Pigs

In 1959, Fidel Castro overthrew the US-backed dictator Batista and took power in Cuba. He nationalised American-owned businesses, which angered the USA. The USA refused to recognise Castro’s government and imposed a trade embargo. Castro turned to the Soviet Union for economic and military support, bringing communism to America’s doorstep — just 90 miles from Florida.

In April 1961, President Kennedy authorised a CIA-backed invasion of Cuba at the Bay of Pigs. Around 1,400 Cuban exiles landed but were quickly defeated by Castro’s forces. The invasion was a humiliating failure that strengthened Castro’s position, pushed Cuba closer to the USSR, and made Kennedy look weak.

The Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962)

In October 1962, American U-2 spy planes photographed Soviet nuclear missile sites being built on Cuba. These missiles could reach most major American cities within minutes. Kennedy faced the most dangerous moment of the entire Cold War.

16 October 1962

Discovery

Kennedy was shown the U-2 photographs. He formed a group of advisers called ExComm to consider the options: a naval blockade, an air strike, an invasion of Cuba, or diplomacy.

22 October 1962

Naval Blockade

Kennedy announced a naval quarantine of Cuba on live television, demanding the removal of Soviet missiles. Soviet ships carrying more missiles were sailing towards Cuba.

24–27 October 1962

Brinkmanship

Soviet ships turned back before reaching the blockade line. Khrushchev sent two letters: the first offered to remove missiles if the USA promised not to invade Cuba; the second demanded the USA also remove its missiles from Turkey. On 27 October, a U-2 spy plane was shot down over Cuba, bringing the world to the brink of nuclear war.

28 October 1962

Resolution

Kennedy agreed to Khrushchev’s first letter (no invasion of Cuba) and secretly agreed to remove US missiles from Turkey. Khrushchev agreed to remove Soviet missiles from Cuba. Nuclear war was averted.

Key Fact

The Cuban Missile Crisis lasted 13 days (16–28 October 1962) and was the closest the world came to nuclear war. Kennedy chose the naval blockade as a middle course — strong enough to pressure the USSR but avoiding a direct military attack that could escalate to nuclear conflict.

Kennedy appeared to win: the Soviet missiles were removed from Cuba, and the USA looked strong. However, Kennedy also secretly agreed to remove US missiles from Turkey and promised never to invade Cuba — concessions that were not made public. Khrushchev could claim he had secured Cuba’s safety and forced the removal of US missiles from Turkey, but he was humiliated domestically and was removed from power in 1964 (partly due to this crisis). Castro was furious at being excluded from the negotiations between Kennedy and Khrushchev.

For example: “Overall, while the Berlin Wall was significant, I would argue that the Cuban Missile Crisis was more important because it was the closest the world came to nuclear war.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Berlin Wall (1961) stopped the refugee crisis but became the defining symbol of Cold War division, remaining in place for 28 years.
  • The Bay of Pigs (1961) was a humiliating failure for Kennedy, pushing Cuba closer to the USSR and setting the stage for the missile crisis.
  • The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) was the closest the world came to nuclear war — resolved through a combination of military pressure and secret diplomacy.

lessons.title: The Prague Spring & International Reactions
lessons.description: Why Czechoslovakia's reforms were crushed, and the consequences of Cuba for arms control.
lessons.content_html:
Opposition in Czechoslovakia

By the late 1960s, Czechoslovakia had been under rigid communist control for twenty years. The economy was stagnating, censorship was strict, and the secret police suppressed all dissent. Many Czechs and Slovaks resented Soviet interference and longed for greater freedom. In January 1968, the reformist leader Alexander Dubček was appointed as leader of the Czechoslovak Communist Party.

The Prague Spring (1968)

Dubček introduced a programme of reforms that became known as the Prague Spring. He wanted to create “socialism with a human face” — keeping communism but making it more humane. His reforms included relaxing censorship to allow greater freedom of speech, allowing other political parties to exist alongside the Communist Party, introducing elements of a market economy, and strengthening trade links with the West.

Key Fact

Unlike Nagy in Hungary (1956), Dubček did not try to leave the Warsaw Pact. He wanted to reform communism, not abandon it. Nevertheless, the Soviet Union saw his reforms as a dangerous threat that could spread to other satellite states.

The Soviet leader Brezhnev feared that if Czechoslovakia’s reforms succeeded, other satellite states would demand similar freedoms — a domino effect that could destroy Soviet control of Eastern Europe. East Germany and Poland, whose leaders were hardline communists, pressured Brezhnev to act. The USSR also worried that relaxed censorship would allow anti-Soviet ideas to spread, and that closer trade links with the West would pull Czechoslovakia out of the Soviet economic orbit.

The Soviet Invasion & the Brezhnev Doctrine

On 20–21 August 1968, around 500,000 Warsaw Pact troops from the USSR, Poland, Hungary, East Germany and Bulgaria invaded Czechoslovakia. There was no armed resistance — Dubček ordered his people not to fight, knowing they could not win against overwhelming force. Instead, Czechs and Slovaks used passive resistance: they removed street signs to confuse invading troops, painted anti-Soviet graffiti, and argued with soldiers.

Dubček was arrested, taken to Moscow, and forced to reverse his reforms. He was eventually replaced by the hardliner Gustáv Husák, who restored rigid communist control. Around 100 Czechs and Slovaks were killed during the invasion, and over 300,000 people fled the country.

Key Fact

The Brezhnev Doctrine declared that the USSR had the right to intervene militarily in any socialist country where communism was threatened. It justified the invasion of Czechoslovakia and sent a clear warning to other satellite states: reform would not be tolerated.

International Reaction to the Soviet Invasion

As with Hungary in 1956, the Western response was limited to verbal condemnation. The USA was heavily involved in the Vietnam War and had no appetite for a direct confrontation with the USSR over Czechoslovakia. NATO condemned the invasion but took no military action. The United Nations debated the crisis, but the USSR used its veto to block any resolution.

However, the invasion had wider consequences. Communist parties in Western Europe, particularly in Italy and France, publicly criticised Moscow, weakening Soviet influence in the West. Romania and Yugoslavia refused to take part in the invasion, showing cracks in Soviet control. Albania left the Warsaw Pact entirely in protest.

Consequences of the Cuban Missile Crisis

The near-catastrophe of the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962 had led both superpowers to take steps to reduce the risk of nuclear war. Several important agreements followed.

1963

The Hotline

A direct communication link (teletype, not a red telephone) was established between the White House and the Kremlin. This meant the leaders could communicate instantly during a crisis, reducing the risk of miscalculation.

1963

Limited Test Ban Treaty

The USA, USSR and Britain agreed to ban nuclear weapons testing in the atmosphere, underwater and in outer space. Underground testing was still allowed. This was the first significant arms control agreement of the Cold War.

1967

Outer Space Treaty

Both superpowers agreed not to place nuclear weapons in space or on the moon. This prevented the arms race from extending beyond Earth.

1968

Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty

The USA, USSR and Britain agreed not to supply nuclear weapons technology to non-nuclear states. This aimed to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons to more countries.

In June 1963, President Kennedy visited West Berlin and delivered his famous “Ich bin ein Berliner” speech to a crowd of 450,000 people. He declared that the Berlin Wall proved the failure of communism: “Freedom has many difficulties and democracy is not perfect, but we have never had to put a wall up to keep our people in.” The speech was a powerful propaganda statement and a reassurance to West Berliners that the USA would not abandon them. It also had a broader significance — it demonstrated continued American commitment to Western Europe despite the improving relations after Cuba.

I know this because the Brezhnev Doctrine stated the USSR had the right to intervene in any socialist country where communism was threatened.” Don’t write too much — two clear points with supporting detail is all that’s needed.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Prague Spring (1968) showed that even moderate reform within communism was unacceptable to the Soviet Union — the Brezhnev Doctrine stated the USSR could intervene in any socialist country where communism was threatened.
  • The West condemned the invasion of Czechoslovakia but took no military action, just as with Hungary in 1956 — containment did not extend to liberating countries already under Soviet control.
  • The consequences of the Cuban Missile Crisis (hotline, Test Ban Treaty, Non-Proliferation Treaty) were the first steps towards reducing Cold War tensions, paving the way for détente in the 1970s.

lessons.title: Détente: SALT, Helsinki & the Limits of Peace
lessons.description: How the superpowers tried to reduce tensions in the 1970s through treaties and agreements.
lessons.content_html:
What Was Détente?

Détente is a French word meaning the relaxation of tension. In the context of the Cold War, it refers to the period during the 1970s when the USA and USSR actively tried to improve relations and reduce the risk of nuclear war. Both superpowers had reasons to pursue détente.

The USA wanted détente because the Vietnam War (1955–75) had been enormously costly in both lives and money, reducing public appetite for confrontation. The arms race was ruinously expensive, and the Cuban Missile Crisis had shown how close the world could come to nuclear destruction. The USSR also wanted to reduce military spending. Its economy was struggling under the burden of the arms race, and the Sino-Soviet split (the breakdown in relations between the USSR and China) meant the USSR now faced potential enemies on two fronts. Both sides recognised that managing their rivalry was safer and cheaper than escalating it.

SALT 1 (1972)

The first Strategic Arms Limitation Talks resulted in SALT 1, signed by President Nixon and Soviet leader Brezhnev in May 1972. The treaty froze the number of ICBMs and submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs) each side could hold at their current levels for five years. It also included the Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty, which limited each side to two missile defence sites.

Key Fact

SALT 1 was significant because it was the first agreement between the superpowers to limit nuclear weapons. However, it only froze existing numbers — it did not reduce them. It also did not cover new technologies like MIRVs (missiles carrying multiple warheads), so the arms race continued in new forms.

The Helsinki Accords (1975)

In August 1975, 35 countries including the USA and USSR signed the Helsinki Accords. These were not a legally binding treaty but a set of agreements covering three areas, known as “baskets.”

Basket 1 — Security: All signatories accepted the post-war borders in Europe, meaning the West formally recognised Soviet control of Eastern Europe. Basket 2 — Economic cooperation: East and West agreed to increase trade, exchange technology and improve transport links. Basket 3 — Human rights: All signatories agreed to respect basic human rights, including freedom of thought, speech and movement.

Key Fact

The Helsinki Accords were the high point of détente. The USSR gained Western recognition of its European borders (Basket 1), but the human rights commitments (Basket 3) later became a powerful tool for dissidents in Eastern Europe to challenge communist governments — something the USSR had not anticipated.

SALT 2 (1979)

Negotiations for a second SALT treaty took seven years. SALT 2 was signed by President Carter and Brezhnev in June 1979. It set equal limits on the number of strategic nuclear delivery vehicles (ICBMs, SLBMs and bombers) each side could hold — a maximum of 2,250 each. It also limited the number of MIRVed missiles.

However, SALT 2 was never ratified by the US Senate. In December 1979, the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan, and Carter withdrew the treaty from Senate consideration as a protest. Détente was effectively over.

Détente reduced tensions but never resolved the fundamental differences between the superpowers. The arms race continued in new forms (MIRVs, cruise missiles). The USSR continued to support communist movements worldwide. The USA continued to support anti-communist governments, even dictatorships. Human rights commitments in the Helsinki Accords were largely ignored by the Soviet Union. When strategic interests clashed — as in Afghanistan — détente collapsed quickly. Critics argued détente was merely a pause, not a genuine peace.

Other Arms Control Treaties

Détente also built on earlier agreements reached after the Cuban Missile Crisis. The Outer Space Treaty (1967) prevented the placement of nuclear weapons in space. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968) aimed to stop the spread of nuclear weapons to non-nuclear states. Together with SALT 1 and the Helsinki Accords, these agreements created a framework of arms control that, while imperfect, helped manage the superpower rivalry throughout the 1970s.

This was because both superpowers were spending huge sums on nuclear weapons, which diverted resources from their economies. As a result, both sides had a financial incentive to agree limits on nuclear weapons, leading to SALT 1 in 1972.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Détente was driven by mutual exhaustion — the cost of the arms race, the Vietnam War, and the Cuban Missile Crisis convinced both sides that managing their rivalry was better than escalating it.
  • SALT 1 (1972) froze missile numbers, and the Helsinki Accords (1975) recognised European borders and included human rights commitments — but SALT 2 was never ratified due to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.
  • Détente reduced tensions but never solved the fundamental ideological divide — when the USSR invaded Afghanistan in 1979, détente collapsed and the “Second Cold War” began.

lessons.title: The Second Cold War: Afghanistan & Reagan’s SDI
lessons.description: How the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and Reagan's policies reignited Cold War tensions.
lessons.content_html:
The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan (1979)

In December 1979, the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan. A communist government had taken power there in 1978, but it faced fierce opposition from Islamic guerrilla fighters known as the mujahideen. When the Afghan government asked for Soviet help, Brezhnev sent over 100,000 troops. He feared that if the communist government fell, it would encourage anti-Soviet movements in the USSR’s own Muslim-majority Central Asian republics.

Key Fact

The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan ended détente and began what historians call the “Second Cold War.” The war lasted ten years (1979–89), cost over 15,000 Soviet soldiers’ lives, and is often compared to America’s experience in Vietnam — a costly, unwinnable guerrilla war.

The USA saw the invasion as Soviet aggression and expansionism. President Carter’s national security adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski warned that the USSR might be trying to reach the oil-rich Persian Gulf. Whether the invasion was genuinely aggressive or merely defensive (protecting a neighbouring communist government) remains debated by historians.

The Carter Doctrine & Western Response

President Carter responded forcefully to the invasion. In January 1980, he announced the Carter Doctrine, declaring that any attempt by an outside force to gain control of the Persian Gulf region would be regarded as an assault on the vital interests of the USA and would be repelled by military force.

Carter also took a series of punitive measures: he withdrew SALT 2 from Senate consideration, imposed a grain embargo on the USSR (cutting off American wheat exports), and increased US defence spending. Most dramatically, the USA boycotted the 1980 Moscow Olympics, with 64 other nations following suit. The USSR retaliated by boycotting the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics.

The 1980 Moscow boycott was led by the USA and included 64 other nations, though some major countries like Britain and France allowed their athletes to compete under the Olympic flag rather than their national flags. The boycott embarrassed the Soviet Union but did not change its policy in Afghanistan. In retaliation, the USSR and 13 allies boycotted the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, claiming concerns about “security” for their athletes. The mutual boycotts showed how deeply the Cold War could penetrate even sport.

The USA also began covertly supplying the mujahideen with weapons and money through Pakistan’s intelligence services. This included Stinger anti-aircraft missiles, which proved devastatingly effective against Soviet helicopters. The CIA’s support for the mujahideen was one of the largest covert operations of the Cold War.

Reagan & the “Second Cold War”

In January 1981, Ronald Reagan became US President. He took a far more aggressive stance towards the Soviet Union than Carter had. Reagan believed détente had been a mistake that allowed the USSR to build up its military while the USA relaxed. He called the Soviet Union an “evil empire” and dramatically increased US defence spending — the military budget rose from $178 billion in 1981 to $229 billion by 1985.

Key Fact

Reagan’s strategy was deliberate: he believed the USA could outspend the Soviet Union in an arms race, forcing the USSR to choose between military spending and economic collapse. The Soviet economy, already struggling, could not match American spending.

The Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI / “Star Wars”)

In March 1983, Reagan announced the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI), nicknamed “Star Wars.” This was a proposed space-based defence system that would use satellites and lasers to shoot down Soviet nuclear missiles before they reached the USA. If it worked, it would make the USA immune to nuclear attack and destroy the principle of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD).

The Soviet Union was alarmed by SDI. If the USA could defend itself against nuclear attack, the USSR’s entire nuclear arsenal would become useless, and the balance of power would shift decisively in America’s favour. Many scientists doubted SDI was technically feasible, and it was never fully built. However, the threat of SDI was enough to worry the Soviet leadership and pressure them into negotiations. SDI became a major obstacle in arms control talks, as the USSR demanded it be abandoned before any new agreements could be reached.

Historians disagree about SDI’s role in ending the Cold War. Some argue that SDI pressured the USSR into negotiations because the Soviet economy could not afford to develop a matching system, ultimately forcing Gorbachev to seek arms reduction deals with the West. Others argue that SDI was never realistic and that the Cold War ended because of the internal weaknesses of the Soviet system and Gorbachev’s own reforms. What is clear is that SDI increased Soviet anxiety and contributed to the sense that the arms race was unsustainable.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (1979) ended détente and triggered the “Second Cold War” — Carter responded with the Carter Doctrine, Olympic boycott, grain embargo, and covert support for the mujahideen.
  • Reagan took an aggressive anti-Soviet stance, dramatically increasing military spending to pressure the weaker Soviet economy and calling the USSR an “evil empire.”
  • The Strategic Defence Initiative (“Star Wars”) alarmed the USSR by threatening to make the USA immune to nuclear attack, pressuring the Soviet leadership into negotiations that would ultimately contribute to the end of the Cold War.

lessons.title: Gorbachev & the Collapse of the Soviet Union
lessons.description: How Gorbachev's reforms led to the fall of the Berlin Wall and the end of the Cold War.
lessons.content_html:
Gorbachev’s “New Thinking”

In March 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev became the leader of the Soviet Union. At 54, he was much younger than his predecessors and brought a fundamentally different approach to governing. Gorbachev recognised that the Soviet Union was in deep trouble: the economy was stagnating, the war in Afghanistan was draining resources and morale, the arms race was cripplingly expensive, and ordinary Soviet citizens faced shortages of basic goods.

Gorbachev introduced what he called “new thinking” — a willingness to reform the Soviet system and to negotiate with the West rather than confront it. His two signature policies were glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring).

Key Fact

Glasnost meant greater freedom of speech, press freedom and political debate. Perestroika meant reforming the economy by reducing central planning and introducing some market-based elements. Gorbachev wanted to modernise the Soviet system, not destroy it — but his reforms ultimately unleashed forces he could not control.

Reducing Cold War Tensions

Gorbachev and Reagan developed a surprisingly productive relationship. Despite their ideological differences, both leaders recognised the need to reduce the nuclear threat. They held a series of summit meetings that transformed the Cold War.

November 1985

Geneva Summit

Gorbachev and Reagan met for the first time. No major agreements were reached, but the two leaders established a personal rapport and agreed to hold further meetings.

October 1986

Reykjavik Summit

Gorbachev proposed eliminating all nuclear weapons within ten years. The talks collapsed because Reagan refused to abandon SDI. However, the summit showed both sides were serious about major arms reductions.

December 1987

INF Treaty

Gorbachev and Reagan signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, eliminating all land-based nuclear missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometres. This was the first treaty to actually reduce (not just limit) nuclear weapons. Nearly 2,700 missiles were destroyed.

Previous agreements (SALT 1, SALT 2) had only limited the growth of nuclear arsenals. The INF Treaty was the first to require the actual destruction of nuclear weapons — nearly 2,700 missiles were eliminated. It included on-site inspections to verify compliance, demonstrating a level of trust that would have been unthinkable a decade earlier. The treaty removed an entire class of weapons from Europe and showed that genuine disarmament was possible.

Impact on Eastern Europe

Gorbachev’s reforms had a transformative effect on Eastern Europe. He made clear that the Soviet Union would no longer use force to keep communist governments in power — effectively abandoning the Brezhnev Doctrine. This was sometimes called the “Sinatra Doctrine” (after Frank Sinatra’s song “My Way”) — satellite states could now go their own way.

Without the threat of Soviet military intervention, opposition movements across Eastern Europe gained momentum. In Poland, the Solidarity trade union movement won free elections in June 1989. In Hungary, the government opened its border with Austria, allowing East Germans to flee west. In Czechoslovakia, the “Velvet Revolution” peacefully removed the communist government. In Romania, the dictator Ceauşescu was overthrown and executed.

The Fall of the Berlin Wall

On 9 November 1989, the Berlin Wall was opened. The East German government, overwhelmed by mass protests and the flood of citizens leaving through Hungary, announced that citizens could cross the border freely. Thousands of jubilant Berliners climbed onto the Wall and began tearing it down with hammers and picks. The event was broadcast live around the world and became the defining image of the end of the Cold War.

Key Fact

The fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 symbolised the end of communist control in Eastern Europe. Germany was formally reunified on 3 October 1990. The Wall that had divided East and West for 28 years was gone.

The Collapse of the Soviet Union

Gorbachev’s reforms, intended to save the Soviet system, ultimately destroyed it. Glasnost allowed people to criticise the government openly for the first time, and many demanded independence for their republics. Perestroika failed to deliver economic improvement, increasing public frustration. Nationalist movements surged in the Baltic states (Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia), Ukraine, and other Soviet republics.

In August 1991, hardline communists attempted a coup against Gorbachev, fearing his reforms had gone too far. The coup failed, largely because Boris Yeltsin (President of the Russian Republic) rallied opposition. However, the failed coup fatally weakened Gorbachev’s authority. One by one, Soviet republics declared independence.

The Warsaw Pact was formally dissolved on 1 July 1991, as its member states had already abandoned communism. On 25 December 1991, Gorbachev resigned as President of the Soviet Union. The following day, 26 December 1991, the Soviet Union was officially dissolved, splitting into 15 independent states. Russia, under Boris Yeltsin, emerged as the largest successor state. The Cold War was over after 46 years.

Key Fact

The Cold War ended not with a military victory but with the internal collapse of the Soviet system. Gorbachev’s reforms, Reagan’s economic pressure, the arms race burden, the Afghan war, nationalist movements, and the fundamental weaknesses of the communist command economy all contributed to the dissolution of the USSR on 26 December 1991.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For “How Far Do You Agree” questions (16 marks) on the end of the Cold War, examiners want you to analyse multiple factors and reach a judgement. Don’t just list factors — compare them. For example: “While Gorbachev’s reforms were important, they would not have succeeded without Reagan’s economic pressure, which forced the USSR to the negotiating table. However, the fundamental weakness of the Soviet economy was arguably the root cause, as it made reform necessary in the first place.” A clear, reasoned conclusion will push you into the top level.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Gorbachev’s glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring) were intended to reform the Soviet system, but they unleashed forces — free speech, nationalist movements, economic expectations — that he could not control.
  • The INF Treaty (1987) was the first agreement to actually reduce nuclear weapons, and the abandonment of the Brezhnev Doctrine allowed Eastern European countries to break free from Soviet control, leading to the fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989.
  • The Soviet Union dissolved on 26 December 1991, ending the Cold War after 46 years — caused by a combination of Gorbachev’s reforms, Reagan’s pressure, the Afghan war, economic weakness, and nationalist movements.

glossary_terms.definition: Soviet leader from 1985 to 1991 who introduced radical reforms (glasnost and perestroika) and sought to reduce Cold War tensions, ultimately overseeing the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
Meaning 'openness' — Gorbachev's policy of allowing greater freedom of speech, press freedom and political debate within the Soviet Union.
Meaning 'restructuring' — Gorbachev's policy of reforming the Soviet economy by introducing some market-based elements and reducing state control.
Reagan's proposed space-based missile defence system, which Gorbachev demanded be abandoned as a condition for further arms reduction.
The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty (1987), which eliminated all land-based nuclear missiles with ranges of 500-5,500 km — the first treaty to actually reduce the number of nuclear weapons.
The Soviet policy that the USSR would intervene in any socialist country where communism was under threat, abandoned by Gorbachev in the late 1980s.
The physical barrier that had divided East and West Berlin since 1961, whose opening on 9 November 1989 became the defining moment of the end of the Cold War.
The failed attempt by hardline communists to overthrow Gorbachev in August 1991, which backfired and accelerated the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
The formal end of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics on 26 December 1991, when the country dissolved into 15 independent states.
